Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

aside adverb

to one side, apart

also take someone aside, draw aside, step aside, call aside, a word in private

classical

Plaut. Aul. 133: eō nunc ego sēcrētō tēd hūc forās sēdūxī
Cic. Att. 5.21.12 (Lewis & Short): mē rūrsus sēdūcit

sēdūcō, sēdūcere, sēdūxī, sēductum

verb, third conjugation, transitive

take (someone) aside

Latin puts “aside” in the prefix sē-, “apart”: sēdūcere, to lead aside; sēvocāre, to call aside; sēcēdere, to step aside. Classically it never means “seduce”: that sense, to lead astray, is Christian Latin (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • sēvocō, sēvocāre, sēvocāvī, sēvocātum — call aside

    verb, first conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Plaut. Men. 1084: sēvocābō erum; Caes. B.G. 5.6 (Lewis & Short): sēvocāre singulōs hortārīque coepit

    A favourite word of Cicero’s (Lewis & Short).

  • sēcēdō, sēcēdere, sēcessī, sēcessum — step aside, withdraw

    verb, third conjugation, intransitive · also used · classical · Plaut. Capt. 263: Sēcēde hūc.; Plaut. Curc. 2.3.2 (Lewis & Short): abīte et dē viā sēcēdite

    Sēcēde hūc, step over here (for a private word), is the comic formula; so concēde hūc (Plaut. Men. 158).

  • seorsum — apart, separately, aside

    adverb · also used · classical

    Apart from the others: Plautus has sēdūxit sōlum sorsum ab aedibus (As. 362), with the old short form. For a word in private, sēcrētō.

Examples

  • Sēcēde hūc. nam sunt quae ex tē sōlō scītārī volō.

    Step aside over here: there are things I want to ask you alone.Plaut. Capt. 263

  • eō nunc ego sēcrētō tēd hūc forās sēdūxī, ut tuam rem ego tēcum hīc loquerer familiārem.

    That’s why I’ve taken you aside out here privately, to talk with you about your family affairs.Plaut. Aul. 133–134

See also save, serious, joke.
